I'm researching peat bog bursts on the area around Crow Hill near Stanbury, West Yorkshire.  I have all the information I need about the 1824 one and about the one in 1989, but I believe there have been others.  
If you have first hand knowledge of other bog bursts in this area (NOT examples of academic research, accounts in the press etc) then I would very much like to hear from you!

Storms in October
We have the real probability of storms in this country and with these there are always power cuts.
POWER CUTS = TURNING ON EMERGENCY BACK UP GENERATION.
It won't be some backup generators switching on nationwide for routine testing, it'll be 6-8GW of backup switching on, 2500 to 3500 generators, probably more.
If the developers get their way like they are currently applying for in the Chapelhall proposal, they'll be used outwith the Emergency Backup regulations. This is unprecedented.
Running at 40% electrical efficiency the thermal power of these generators will be 15-20 GW of thermal heat. What was the point of leaving trillions of tonnes of coal and closing power stations only to use diesel, gas or (ha ha) HVO instead?
So as the Central Belt is asphyxiated by pollution, deafened by noise, drained of more drinking water for increased cooling and paralysed by power outages at least,according to Mark Wilson of ILI the surrounding lands will be heated up for tomato growing. Two and a half times more thermal waste from backup generation..... 99.9998% reliable, aye ok.

records.title: Scotland Against Spin
records.bodyText:
Herald letters
G DUNCAN writes that “the future is electric” and that we must shut down all fossil fuel production. While the electric motor is a wonderful thing, we will need more oil and gas far into the next century and I will explain why.
We need coal to make quality steel, oil as a lubricant, hydrocarbons for plastics, and gas for operating highly efficient domestic boilers which can heat your home in hours, not days like heat pumps after you return from an autumn break.
Did you return on a jet after your holiday? Battery-powered like an EV? Er, no. Jet engines are powered by Jet A-1, which doesn’t freeze until -47C or Jet B which doesn’t freeze until -72C, whereas batteries will lose efficiency at freezing point and freeze solid at -20C. If the temperature at sea level is 8C, it will be -44C at 8,000 metres. So, no airline will use battery-powered aircraft. And batteries themselves are made of plastic made from oil, and metals mined by diesel power.
Thinking of an EV? Without hydrocarbons there would be no EVS.
Thinking of a newbuild? Then you need cement which is made using coal burned at 1,450C, and the roadways surfaced with tar, made from coal. Geologists have now discovered a one trillion-ton deposit under the Firth of Forth – one of many huge deposits in the UK – but, of course, politicians prefer to import coal from Columbia than mine it in Scotland, Yorkshire or Nottingham.
Looking forward to dualling the A9? Try that without diesel power, cement, steel and asphalt.
Been to Specsavers? Your specs are made from oil and gas derivatives. Sore head? Aspirin is made from benzene. Going for an op? Impossible without plastics, chemicals, and gases made from hydrocarbons. The list of useful products made from hydrocarbons is endless.
Yet the electronic sandwich board wearers demand we shut down all oil, gas and coal production to “prevent climate change”. They rejoice in the phrase “fossil fuels” as if they belonged in, rather than emerged from, an ancient prehistoric epoch. I do not believe we can control the climate and there are many benefits from climate change for Scotland such as warmer summers and milder winters.
Thanks to the foolish net-zero policies of successive governments, the UK now depends on Norway for oil and gas for half its needs. Norway is continuing to licence new oil and gas fields and redevelop old ones with new technology in the same geology as the UK’S fields are. Let’s choose reality over ideology. Rosebank and Jackdaw must be initiated now.
William Loneskie, Berwickshire.
I FULLY support Dave Morris in his wish that more should be done to protect Scotland’s Wild Land Areas, which he calls “some of Europe’s most cherished wild places”.
He bemoans their degradation through the current vogue for onshore wind farms, and argues that a change in energy policy is urgently needed.
But it is not only wind farms which are causing an attrition of our wild areas: forestry, indeed tree-planting schemes generally, are also changing the nature of these landscapes, introducing a new human-planned element.
What would the Gaelic poet Duncan Ban Macintyre have made of all this, a poet who celebrated the nature of his beloved hills? In his song Last Farewell to the Mountains (translated from Gaelic by Anne Lorne Gillies), he sings: “Fairwell to the deer forests,
Oh! What wonderful mountains they are…
The moors which are so precious, And the pastures which are so plentiful,
Oh, joyfully I take my leave of them – My final blessings to them forever.” Or, to quote Sir Walter Scott: “What makes Scotland Scotland is fast disappearing.”
Our distinctive landscapes are cherished by both residents and visitors alike, and the Charter for the Open Hill is an initiative set up to encourage the Scottish Government to safeguard them – so that they are still there to be enjoyed by future generations.
Everyone is encouraged to sign the Charter.
James Fenton,
Oban.

records.bodyText:
Building new utility-scale solar farms often faces two huge bottlenecks: clearing valuable farmland and waiting years to build expensive high-voltage transmission lines to connect to the power grid.
On the Alqueva reservoir in southern Portugal - Western Europe's largest artificial lake engineers at EDP created a triple-hybrid energy island by floating 12,000 photovoltaic panels right beside an existing hydroelectric dam.
Instead of using pure virgin plastic floats, engineers teamed up with Portuguese cork manufacturer Corticeira Amorim to mold the four- hectare floating island from a carbon-negative composite of native cork and recycled polymers.
During hot, sunny summer afternoons, the cool reservoir water underneath chills the floating panels to boost their electrical output by 10% while shading the reservoir surface to prevent precious fresh water from evaporating.
Best of all, the floating solar island, the hydroelectric turbines, and an onshore battery bank all plug into the exact same grid substation - letting Portugal use solar by day and save hydro water for the night.— in Portugal.
